extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists, policy-makers, and general readers interested in the theory of rent, wages, and interest
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains nineteenth-century political-economy principles about economic rent, the law of rent (Ricardo), the relation between rent, wages and interest, and the philosophical/causal account of interest. The material is a chapter-length exposition intended to define terms and deduce corollaries for distribution of wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic definition of rent
rubrics_metrics.description: The term rent, in its economic sense, denotes that part of the produce which accrues to the owners of land or other natural capabilities by virtue of their ownership; it differs from common usage and is narrower in excluding payments for the use of products of human exertion, and wider in including cases where owner and user are the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the portion of payments attributable to the use of bare land or natural capabilities is economic rent; payments for use of buildings, machinery, or other improvements are classified as interest (consideration for use of capital). Rent can be actual (land in use) or potential (land has value though unused). When land is bought, the purchase price is rent capitalized. The value of land (and rent) exists only because ownership confers the power to secure part of production; land has no value until someone is willing to give labor or its products for its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rent as price of monopoly (source of land value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent is the price of monopoly arising from the reduction to individual ownership of natural elements which human exertion can neither produce nor increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rent depends on comparative availability: a very productive parcel yields no rent if equally good land is freely available. When superior land becomes scarce (others appropriated), its owner can obtain rent. If one owner controlled all accessible land, he could demand any terms; under widespread individual ownership, market rent is limited by competition among owners. The capacity to yield rent is what gives land its exchange value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of rent (Ricardo's law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rent of land is determined by the excess of its produce over that which the same application can secure from the least productive land in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to all natural agencies (mines, fisheries, etc.), not only agriculture. The law follows from competition pushing wages and interest to a common level; owners of more productive land appropriate as rent whatever exceeds the ordinary return obtainable on the least productive land in use (the margin of cultivation). Alternate phrasing: ownership confers power to appropriate so much of the wealth produced as exceeds the return labor and capital could secure on the poorest natural opportunities free to them. Examples and algebraic form (Produce = Rent + Wages + Interest; hence Produce − Rent = Wages + Interest) elucidate the relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: rent determines wages and interest (Produce − Rent = Wages + Interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because rent appropriates the excess above the margin, wages and interest are whatever remains after rent is taken; wages and interest do not depend on total productive power but on produce attainable without paying rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If increased productive power is matched by proportional increases in land value (rent), wages and interest remain unchanged; if rent increases faster, wages and interest may fall. This explains observed facts: new countries with low land values can have high wages and interest despite low production, while old countries with high land values can have large production but low wages and interest. The 'rent line' (margin of cultivation) fixes the portion of produce available to labor and capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital as stored-up labor and its subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is but stored-up labor (a form of labor), and its law must be subordinate to, and independently correlate with, the law of wages so as to fit cases where production involves labor and capital without rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because labor applied to land can produce wealth without capital (capital is not a necessary factor), laws of rent and wages can form a consistent framework even absent capital. Capital's returns (interest) are conceptually distinct from rent and must be derived to correlate with wages and rent in various cases (e.g., when the whole produce divides only between labor and capital).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of interest in distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest, as an abstract term in the distribution of wealth, includes all returns for the use of capital and excludes compensation for risk (which affects observed commercial rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed differences in nominal interest largely reflect risk differentials; the underlying general rate of interest (interest proper) varies between places and over time (e.g., higher historically in the U.S. than England, and higher in newer states). Interest proper does not depend simply on productiveness of labor and capital or inversely on wages; empirical patterns show interest low where productivity is high and high where wages are high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of 'interest as reward of abstinence'
rubrics_metrics.description: The common justification that interest is the reward of abstinence (the lender's sacrifice of consumption) is inadequate: abstinence alone produces nothing and does not logically require a surplus return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bastiat's plane-and-plank illustration is analyzed to show the fallacy: lending a tool per se does not transfer increased productive power or justify surplus without further causal elements. Pure abstinence (simply not consuming) would not by itself yield an increase; examples where lending yields no net loss to lender (simple return of tool) show abstinence is not a sufficient explanation. The text argues that basing interest on abstinence leads to contradictions and social objections (interest as robbery of labor) and that other causal factors must be sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of interest: reproductive forces of nature and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest springs from the active, separable power of nature (the principle of growth/reproduction) and the element of time — certain species of capital, or uses of capital, will by nature or exchange produce an increase over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: wine improves in value with time, bees and livestock reproduce, seeds yield crops; differences in location/production (comparative advantages) exploited by exchange can yield gains (trade increases returns). The element of time makes it necessary that a lender receive more than mere return of identical goods when those goods could have been put to reproductive uses. Interchangeability of wealth leads to an averaging of the advantage from species that reproduce, so the lender of money or inert goods is not deprived of an expected increase because the market averages reproductive returns across forms of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between labor-only production and time/reproduction-based production
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a qualitative distinction between modes of production that depend solely on labor (where production stops when labor stops and time is not an element) and modes that utilize reproductive forces of nature or distributional differences (where time is an essential element and production continues or increases while labor is not continuously applied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In labor-only production (e.g., planing boards, factory work, mining), stopping labor stops production immediately; time between labor bouts adds nothing. In production harnessing reproductive forces (agriculture, breeding, fermentation, exploitation of locational differences), time itself contributes to output (growth, reproduction, compound gains). This distinction explains why time (and thus interest) matters in some productions but not others, and underpins the causal account of interest given above.
